L13: cite9†Image: A Few Lessons for Investors and Managers L14: # A Few Lessons for Investors and Managers
L15: #### from Warren E. Buffett
L16: 
L17: By Peter Bevelin
L18: 
L19: Peter Bevelin begins A Few Lessons for Investors and Managers with Warren Buffett’s wisdom, "I am a better investor because I am a businessman and a better businessman because I am an investor." This book is about how managers and investors can increase their chance of success and reduce the chance of harm if managers think more like investors and investors more like businessmen.
L20: There are a lot of books about Warren Buffett, but A Few Lessons for Investors and Managers is different. It tells in a short-easy-to-read way about what managers and investors can learn from Buffett.
L21: This is a selection of useful and timeless wisdom where Warren Buffett in his own words tells us how to think about business valuation, what is a good and bad business, acquisitions and their traps, yardsticks, compensation issues, how to reduce risk, corporate governance, the importance of trust and the right culture, learning from mistakes, and more.

L85:     PREFACE
L86:     PREFACE
L87:     During the past twenty years there has been an extraordinary
L88:     growth of interest in Zen Buddhism. Since the Second World War
L89:     this interest has increased so much that it seems to be becoming a
L90:     considerable force in the intellectual and artistic world of the West.
L91:     It is connected, no doubt, with the prevalent enthusiasm for
L92:     Japanese culture which is one of the constructive results of the late
L93:     war, but which may amount to no more than a passing fashion. The
L94:     deeper reason for this interest is that the viewpoint of Zen lies so
L95:     close to the “growing edge” of Western thought.
L96:     The more alarming and destructive aspects of Western civilization
L97:     should not blind us to the fact that at this very time it is also in one
L98:     of its most creative periods. Ideas and insights of the greatest
L99:     fascination are appearing in some of the newer elds of Western
L100:     science–in psychology and psychotherapy, in logic and the
L101:     philosophy of science, in semantics and communications theory.
L102:     Some of these developments might be due to suggestive in uences
L103:     from Asian philosophy, but on the whole I am inclined to feel that
L104:     there is more of a parallelism than a direct in uence. We are,
L105:     however, becoming aware of the parallelism, and it promises an
L106:     exchange of views which should be extremely stimulating.
L107:     Western thought has changed so rapidly in this century that we
L108:     are in a state of considerable confusion. Not only are there serious
L109:     di culties of communication between the intellectual and the
L110:     general public, but the course of our thinking and of our very
L111:     history has seriously undermined the common-sense assumptions
L112:     which lie at the roots of our social conventions and institutions.
L113:     Familiar concepts of space, time, and motion, of nature and natural
L114:     law, of history and social change, and of human personality itself
L115:     have dissolved, and we nd ourselves adrift without landmarks in a
L116:     universe which more and more resembles the Buddhist principle of
L117:     the “Great Void.” The various wisdoms of the West, religious,
L118:     philosophical, and scienti c, do not o er much guidance to the art
L119:     philosophical, and scienti c, do not o er much guidance to the art
L120:     of living in such a universe, and we nd the prospects of making
L121:     our way in so trackless an ocean of relativity rather frightening. For
L122:     we are used to absolutes, to rm principles and laws to which we
L123:     can cling for spiritual and psychological security.
L124:     This is why, I think, there is so much interest in a culturally
L125:     productive way of life which, for some fteen hundred years, has
L126:     felt thoroughly at home in “the Void,” and which not only feels no
L127:     terror for it but rather a positive delight. To use its own words, the
L128:     situation of Zen has always been–
L129:     Above, not a tile to cover the head;
L130:     Below, not an inch of ground for the foot.
L131:     Such language should not actually be so unfamiliar to us, were we
L132:     truly prepared to accept the meaning of “the foxes have holes, and
L133:     the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man hath not where
L134:     to lay his head.”
L135:     I am not in favor of “importing” Zen from the Far East, for it has
L136:     become deeply involved with cultural institutions which are quite
L137:     foreign to us. But there is no doubt that there are things which we
L138:     can learn, or unlearn, from it and apply in our own way. It has the
L139:     special merit of a mode of expressing itself which is as intelligible–
L140:     or perhaps as ba ing–to the intellectual as to the illiterate, o ering
L141:     possibilities of communication which we have not explored. It has
L142:     a directness, verve, and humor, and a sense of both beauty and
L143:     nonsense at once exasperating and delightful. But above all it has a
L144:     way of being able to turn one’s mind inside out, and dissolving
L145:     what seemed to be the most oppressive human problems into
L146:     questions like “Why is a mouse when it spins?” At its heart there is
L147:     a strong but completely unsentimental compassion for human
L148:     beings su ering and perishing from their very attempts to save
L149:     themselves.
L150:     There are many excellent books about Zen, though some of the
L151:     best are out of print or otherwise di cult to obtain. But as yet no
L152:     one–not even Professor Suzuki—has given us a comprehensive
L153:     account of the subject which includes its historical background and
L154:     account of the subject which includes its historical background and
L155:     its relation to Chinese and Indian ways of thought. The three
L156:     volumes of Suzuki’s Essays in Zen Buddhism are an unsystematic
L157:     collection of scholarly papers on various aspects of the subject,
L158:     enormously useful for the advanced student but quite ba ing to the
L159:     general reader without an understanding of the general principles.
L160:     His delightful Introduction to Zen Buddhism is rather narrow and
L161:     specialized. It omits the essential information about the relation of
L162:     Zen to Chinese Taoism and Indian Buddhism, and is in some
L163:     respects rather more mystifying than it need be. His other works are
L164:     studies of special aspects of Zen, all of which require general
L165:     background and historical perspective.
L166:     R. H. Blyth’s Zen in English Literature and Oriental Classics is one
L167:     of the best introductions available, but it is published only in Japan
L168:     and, again, lacks the background information. As a series of
L169:     rambling and marvelously perceptive observations, it makes no
L170:     attempt to give an orderly presentation of the subject. My own
L171:     Spirit of Zen is a popularization of Suzuki’s earlier works, and
L172:     besides being very unscholarly it is in many respects out of date and
L173:     misleading, whatever merits it may have in the way of lucidity and
L174:     simplicity. Christmas Humphreys’ Zen Buddhism, published only in
L175:     England, is likewise a popularization of Suzuki and, once more,
L176:     does not really begin to put Zen in its cultural context. It is written
L177:     in a clear and sprightly fashion, but the author nds identities
L178:     between Buddhism and Theosophy which I feel to be highly
L179:     questionable. Other studies of Zen by both Western and Asian
L180:     authors are of a more specialized character, or are discussions of
L181:     Zen à propos of something else–psychology, art, or cultural history.
L182:     In default, then, of a fundamental, orderly, and comprehensive
L183:     account of the subject, it is no wonder that Western impressions of
L184:     Zen are somewhat confused, despite all the enthusiasm and interest
L185:     which it has aroused. The problem, then, is to write such a book–
L186:     and this I have tried to do since no one who understands the subject
L187:     better than I seems willing or able to do so. Ideally, I suppose, such
L188:     a work should be written by an accomplished and recognized Zen
L189:     master. But at present no such person has su cient command of
L190:     English. Furthermore, when one speaks from within a tradition, and
L191:     English. Furthermore, when one speaks from within a tradition, and
L192:     especially from within its institutional hierarchy, there is always apt
L193:     to be a certain lack of perspective and grasp of the outsider’s
L194:     viewpoint. Again, one of the biggest obstacles to communication
L195:     between Japanese Zen masters and Westerners is the absence of
L196:     clarity as to di erence of basic cultural premises. Both sides are so
L197:     “set in their ways” that they are unaware of the limitations of their
L198:     means of communication.
L199:     Perhaps, then, the most appropriate author of such a work would
L200:     be a Westerner who had spent some years under a Japanese master,
L201:     going through the whole course of Zen training. Now from the
L202:     standpoint of Western “scienti c scholarship” this would not do at
L203:     all, for such a person would have become an “enthusiast” and
L204:     “partisan” incapable of an objective and disinterested view. But,
L205:     fortunately or unfortunately, Zen is above all an experience,
L206:     nonverbal in character, which is simply inaccessible to the purely
L207:     literary and scholarly approach. To know what Zen is, and
L208:     especially what it is not, there is no alternative but to practice it, to
L209:     experiment with it in the concrete so as to discover the meaning
L210:     which underlies the words. Yet such Westerners as have undergone
L211:     some of the special type of training followed in Rinzai Zen tend to
L212:     become “cagey” and uncommunicative on the principle that
L213:     Those who know do not speak;
L214:     Those who speak do not know.
L215:     Although, however, they do not “put up,” they do not completely
L216:     “shut up.” On the one hand, they would love to share their
L217:     understanding with others. But on the other hand, they are
L218:     convinced that words are ultimately futile, and are, furthermore,
L219:     under an agreement not to discuss certain aspects of their training.
L220:     They begin, therefore, to take the characteristically Asian attitude of
L221:     “Come and nd out for yourself.” But the scienti cally trained
L222:     Westerner is, not without reason, a cautious and skeptical fellow
L223:     who likes to know what he is “getting into.” He is acutely conscious
L224:     of the capacity of the mind for self-deception, for going into places
L225:     where entrance is impossible without leaving one’s critical
L226:     where entrance is impossible without leaving one’s critical
L227:     perspective at the door. Asians tend so much to despise this
L228:     attitude, and their Western devotees even more so, that they neglect
L229:     to tell the scienti c inquirer many things that are still well within
L230:     the possibilities of human speech and intellectual understanding.
L231:     To write about Zen is, therefore, as problematic for the outside,
L232:     “objective” observer as for the inside, “subjective” disciple. In
L233:     varying situations I have found myself on both sides of the
L234:     dilemma. I have associated and studied with the “objective
L235:     observers” and am convinced that, for all their virtues, they
L236:     invariably miss the point and eat the menu instead of the dinner. I
L237:     have also been on the inside of a traditional hierarchy–not Zen–and
L238:     am equally convinced that from this position one does not know
L239:     what dinner is being eaten. In such a position one becomes
L240:     technically “idiotic,” which is to say, out of communication with
L241:     those who do not belong to the same fold.
L242:     It is both dangerous and absurd for our world to be a group of
L243:     communions mutually excommunicate. This is especially true of the
L244:     great cultures of the East and the West, where the potentialities of
L245:     communication are the richest, and the dangers of failure to
L246:     communicate the worst. As one who has spent somewhat more than
L247:     twenty years trying to interpret the East to the West, I have become
L248:     increasingly certain that to interpret such a phenomenon as Zen
L249:     there is a clear principle to be followed. On the one hand, it is
L250:     necessary to be sympathetic and to experiment personally with the
L251:     way of life to the limit of one’s possibilities. On the other hand, one
L252:     must resist every temptation to “join the organization,” to become
L253:     involved with its institutional commitments. In this friendly neutral
L254:     position one is apt to be disowned by both sides. But, at the worst,
L255:     one’s misrepresentations provoke them to express themselves more
L256:     clearly. For the relationship between two positions becomes far
L257:     more clear when there is a third with which to compare them. Thus
L258:     even if this study of Zen does no more than express a standpoint
L259:     which is neither Zen nor anything Western, it will at least provide
L260:     that third point of reference.
L261:     However, there can be no doubt that the essential standpoint of
L262:     Zen refuses to be organized, or to be made the exclusive possession
L263:     Zen refuses to be organized, or to be made the exclusive possession
L264:     of any institution. If there is anything in this world which transcends
L265:     the relativities of cultural conditioning, it is Zen–by whatever name
L266:     it may be called. This is an excellent reason for Zen’s not being
L267:     institutionalized, and for the fact that many of its ancient exponents
L268:     were “universal individualists” who were never members of any
L269:     Zen organization, and never sought the acknowledgment of any
L270:     formal authority.
L271:     This, then, is my position with respect to Zen–and I feel I should
L272:     be frank with the reader in a day when there is so much anxiety
L273:     about people’s credentials or “quanti cations.” I cannot represent
L274:     myself as a Zenist, or even as a Buddhist, for this seems to me to be
L275:     like trying to wrap up and label the sky. I cannot represent myself
L276:     as a scienti cally objective academician, for–with respect to Zen–
L277:     this seems to me to be like studying bird–song in a collection of
L278:     stu ed nightingales. I claim no rights to speak of Zen. I claim only
L279:     the pleasure of having studied its literature and observed its art
L280:     forms since I was hardly more than a boy, and of having had the
L281:     delight of informal association with a number of Japanese and
L282:     Chinese travelers of the same trackless way.
L283:     This book is intended both for the general reader and for the
L284:     more serious student, and I trust that the former will be tolerant of
L285:     the use of some technical terminology, a Chinese character
L286:     appendix, and other critical apparatus most useful for those who
L287:     wish to explore the subject more deeply. The book is divided into
L288:     two parts, the rst dealing with the background and history of Zen,
L289:     and the second with its principles and practice. The sources of
L290:     information are of three types. I have, rstly, used almost all the
L291:     studies of Zen in European languages. Naturally, I have made
L292:     considerable use of the works of Professor D. T. Suzuki, but at the
L293:     same time I have tried not to rely upon them too heavily–not
L294:     because of any defect in them, but because I think readers are
L295:     entitled to something more, by way of a fresh viewpoint, than a
L296:     mere summarization of his views.
L297:     Secondly, I have based the essential view of Zen here presented
L298:     upon a careful study of the more important of its early Chinese
L299:     records, with special reference to the Hsin-hsin Ming, the T’an
L300:     records, with special reference to the Hsin-hsin Ming, the T’an
L301:     Ching or Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, the Lin-chi Lu, and the Kutsun-hsü Yü-lu. My own knowledge of T’ang dynasty Chinese is
L302:     certainly not enough to deal with some of the ner points of this
L303:     literature, but su cient, I think, to get what I wanted, which was a
L304:     clear view of the essential doctrine. In all this, my e orts have been
L305:     greatly aided by colleagues and research associates at the American
L306:     Academy of Asian Studies, and I wish in particular to express my
L307:     thanks to Professors Sabro Hasegawa and Gi-ming Shien, to Dr. Paul
L308:     and Dr. George Fung, Dr. Frederick Hong, Mr. Charles Yick, and to
L309:     Mr. Kazumitsu Kato, priest of the Soto-Zen School.
L310:     Thirdly, my information is derived from a large number of
L311:     personal encounters with teachers and students of Zen, spread over
L312:     more than twenty years.
L313:     In the following pages the translations from the original texts are
L314:     my own, unless otherwise indicated. For the convenience of those
L315:     who read Chinese, I have supplied, following the Bibliography, an
L316:     appendix of the original Chinese forms of the more important
L317:     quotations and technical terms. I have found these almost essential
L318:     for the more serious student, for even among the most highly
L319:     quali ed scholars there is still much uncertainty as to the proper
L320:     translation of T’ang dynasty Zen texts. References to this appendix
L321:     are by superscribed index letters in alphabetical order.
L322:     References to other works are by surname of the author and
L323:     number, directing the reader to the Bibliography for full details.
L324:     Scholarly readers will have to excuse me for not using the absurd
L325:     diacritical marks in romanized Sanskrit words, since these are
L326:     merely confusing to the general reader and unnecessary to the
L327:     Sanskritist who will at once call to mind the Devanagiri script. As to
L328:     the proper names of Zen masters and titles of Zen texts, these are
L329:     given in the romanized forms of Mandarin or Japanese according to
L330:     the country of origin, and technical terms are given in Mandarin
L331:     unless used in the discussion of speci cally Japanese Zen. For
L332:     Mandarin one is almost compelled by general usage to adopt the
L333:     Wade-Giles romanization, for which I have appended a table of
L334:     pronunciation following this Preface, since it has so little relation to
L335:     the actual sounds.
L336:     the actual sounds.
L337:     I am most grateful to Mr. R. H. Blyth for his kind permission to
L338:     quote a number of his translations of haiku poems from his
L339:     magni cent four-volume anthology, Haiku, published by the
L340:     Hokuseido Press in Tokyo; to Professor Sabro Hasegawa for his
L341:     generous help in preparing the jacket and providing illustrations;
L342:     and to my daughter Joan for the photographs of Ryoanji.
L343:     In conclusion, I am most happy to express my thanks to the
L344:     Bollingen Foundation for a three-year fellowship, during which
L345:     much of the preliminary study was done for the writing of this
L346:     book.
L347:     ALAN W. WATTS

L384:     PART ONE
L385:     BACKGROUND AND HISTORY
L386:     One
L387:     THE PHILOSOPHY OF THE TAO
L388:     Zen Buddhism is a way and a view of life which does not belong to
L389:     any of the formal categories of modern Western thought. It is not
L390:     religion or philosophy; it is not a psychology or a type of science. It
L391:     is an example of what is known in India and China as a “way of
L392:     liberation,” and is similar in this respect to Taoism, Vedanta, and
L393:     Yoga. As will soon be obvious, a way of liberation can have no

L113: A wide-ranging, interdisciplinary look at global changes that may occur over the next fifty years—whether sudden and cataclysmic world-changing events or gradually unfolding trends.
L114: Fundamental change occurs most often in one of two ways: as a “fatal discontinuity,” a sudden catastrophic event that is potentially world changing, or as a persistent, gradual trend. Global catastrophes include volcanic eruptions, viral pandemics, wars, and large-scale terrorist attacks; trends are demographic, environmental, economic, and political shifts that unfold over time.
L115: In this provocative book, scientist Vaclav Smil takes a wide-ranging, interdisciplinary look at the catastrophes and trends the next fifty years may bring.
L116: Smil first looks at rare but cataclysmic events, both natural and human-produced, then at trends of global importance, including the transition from fossil fuels to other energy sources and growing economic and social inequality. He also considers environmental change—in some ways an amalgam of sudden discontinuities and gradual change—and assesses the often misunderstood complexities of global warming.
L117: Global Catastrophes and Trends does not come down on the side of either doom-and-gloom scenarios or techno-euphoria. Instead, Smil argues that understanding change will help us reverse negative trends and minimize the risk of catastrophe.
L118: Vaclav Smil is Distinguished Professor Emeritus at the University of Manitoba. He is the author of forty books, including New York Times bestseller How the World Really Works and Energy and Civilization, published by the MIT Press. In 2010 he was named by Foreign Policy as one of the Top 100 Global Thinkers. In 2013 Bill Gates wrote on his website that “there is no author whose books I look forward to more than Vaclav Smil.
L119: > I think Smil should probably be set as homework for every Member of Parliament, and there will be a test later... ~Dick Pountain, The Political Quarterly
L120: > At home alike in both the natural and human sciences, the author gives an incisive analysis of the way change occurs both in terms of unpredictable discontinuities and gradually unfolding trends. His treatment of trends over the next fifty years is especially interesting, and his pages on America's 'retreat' informed and convincing. Smil offers not predictions but a balanced, holistic treatment of what may be ahead for humanity.
L121: Anyone interested in history, demography, economics, environmentalism, or risk analysis, along with globalization, will find this a 'must' book. ~Bruce Mazlish, Professor of History Emeritus, MIT

Intellectuals and Society is a non-fiction book by Thomas Sowell. The book was initially published on January 5, 2010, by Basic Books.

Intellectuals are defined as "idea workers" who exercise profound influence on policy makers and public opinion, but are often not directly accountable for the results. Intellectuals and Society examines the record of these idea workers and the conditions, methods and incentives driving their points of view that, according to Sowell, have often resulted in disaster for societies where intellectuals have been allowed "undue influence".

# The Intellectual Life and the Social Life: Imperfect Together

June 12, 2018 by Will Morrisey

Thomas Sowell: Intellectuals and Society. New York: Basic Books, 2009.

Originally published in Social Science and Modern Society. Volume 47, Number 6, November/December 2010.

The respected conservative economist Thomas Sowell writes too gracefully and, well, economically to offer a more precise title for this book, such as Modern Intellectuals and Modern Democratic Regimes. But that’s his topic.

By “intellect” Sowell means “the capacity to grasp and manipulate complex ideas.” Intellect forms only part of “intelligence,” a term encompassing “judgment and care in selecting relevant explanatory facts and in establishing empirical tests of any theory that emerges.” A bright college sophomore’s intellect ought to metamorphose into intelligence by the time he starts his doctoral dissertation. December 7, 2006 | Read Time: 14 minutes

In his new book, The Foundation: A Great American Secret — How Private Wealth Is Changing the World, Joel L. Fleishman, a professor at Duke University, offers ideas on how to make grant makers more accountable. Following is an excerpt from the book, which will be released next month by PublicAffairs:

Foundations have an overriding obligation to the public to perform their duties according to the highest standards of stewardship. That obligation arises from the tax deductibility of gifts to create foundations and the tax-exempt status granted to foundation assets and income once they are established. As a result of these benefits, United States taxpayers annually benefit United States foundations with foregone taxes in excess of $20-billion.
